## Eight common assumptions, negated

| # | Common assumption | If it were false, the conditional effect would be |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | L2 strength is set by alpha alone, regardless of batch size. | In sklearn the L2 term is scaled by 1/B per step, so the effective per-epoch decay is about alpha·N/B². Raising alpha would then hurt much more at small B and be close to harmless at large B. |
| A2 | Adam's per-parameter normalization makes the learning rate width-independent. | Adam's update size per weight is fixed, so a wider layer moves its outputs more per step. A higher learning rate would hurt more at high width and help more at low width. |
| A3 | Wider is always better, because overparameterization regularizes implicitly. | The total L2 penalty grows with parameter count. Widening would then help less when alpha is high and more when alpha is low. |
| A4 | Batch size mainly trades off speed against noise and is roughly neutral for accuracy. | With a fixed 243-epoch budget, larger B means fewer steps. Larger B would hurt at low learning rate but stabilize Adam at high learning rate, especially in deep nets. |
| A5 | Depth is a pure capacity knob that does not depend on the optimizer settings. | Instability compounds across layers. Adding depth would hurt more at high learning rate and with noisy small-batch gradients, but help when layers are narrow. |
| A6 | Regularization is more valuable in larger models. | A shallow network underfits, so adding alpha would hurt there. A wide network would benefit from extra alpha. |
| A7 | Width and depth are interchangeable ways to add capacity. | If they substitute for each other, removing width matters most when there is only one layer. |
| A8 | Lowering the learning rate is "safe" and at worst slower. | Within 243 epochs, deep nets at low learning rate fail to finish training. More steps (smaller B) would then help at a moderate learning rate. |

## Hypotheses (summary)

1. **alpha↑ | batch low → lower.** Effective decay scales as alpha·N/B², so small batches over-shrink the weights. *(A1)*
2. **alpha↑ | batch high → higher.** At large batch sizes the effective decay is negligible. *(A1)*
3. **lr↑ | width high → lower.** Under standard parametrization, the output change per Adam step grows with width. *(A2)*
4. **lr↑ | width low → higher.** Narrow nets need larger steps to move their outputs. *(A2)*
5. **width↑ | alpha high → lower.** The total penalty grows with the number of parameters. *(A3)*
6. **width↑ | alpha low → higher.** Without much L2, implicit regularization from width dominates. *(A3)*
7. **batch↑ | lr high → higher.** Averaging over more samples damps updates that would otherwise diverge. *(A4)*
8. **batch↑ | lr low → lower.** Losing update steps is costly when each step is small. *(A4)*
9. **batch↑ | depth high → higher.** The stabilizing rescue matters more in deep nets. *(A4)*
10. **depth↑ | lr high → lower.** Instability compounds across layers. *(A5)*
11. **depth↑ | batch low → lower.** Gradient noise is amplified through more layers. *(A5)*
12. **lr↑ | batch high → higher.** Larger batches tolerate a larger learning rate and need it to cover the reduced step count. *(A4)*
13. **lr↓ | depth high → lower.** Deep nets fail to finish training within the epoch budget. *(A8)*
14. **width↑ | lr low → higher.** Width acts as an implicit learning-rate multiplier under Adam. *(A2)*
15. **alpha↑ | width high → higher.** Large nets that overfit gain the most from regularization. *(A6)*
16. **alpha↑ | depth low → lower.** Shallow nets underfit, so extra regularization only hurts. *(A6)*
17. **depth↑ | alpha high → lower.** Shrunk weights multiply across layers and collapse the signal. *(A3, A5)*
18. **width↓ | depth low → lower.** With one layer, width is the only capacity route. *(A7)*
19. **depth↑ | width low → higher.** Depth relieves the narrow-layer bottleneck. *(A7)*
20. **batch↓ | lr mid → higher.** More steps help when the learning rate is moderate. *(A8)*
